name: opencode abort vs Task cancelled semantics
observations: opencode records BOTH user ESC and internal cancellation as MessageAbortedError on the message row, with error=Aborted in the log. It does NOT record who called the abort endpoint.

message table time_created = when processing STARTED, time_updated = when it ended/was aborted. Use time_updated on message rows to find true death times.

Two easy-to-get-wrong domain rules: a formula's on-disk dir is Cellar/<name>/<keg_version> where keg_version() appends _<revision> when revision > 0 (1181 of 8617 formulae have one); is_installed is name-only because the upstream API's dependencies array is a flat list of names with zero constraint syntax across all 8617 entries - that is a feed limitation, not an oversight.

Synthetic FormulaRecord fixtures once hid a bug that broke every install (uses_from_macos is a heterogeneous array in the real feed, typed as Vec<String>). 90 unit tests stayed green. Always exercise a real install against the live index with CLAY_PREFIX=/tmp/clay-check before trusting formula parsing or resolution.

The real path-traversal vector in install_from_source was the VERSION, not the name: keg_version() comes straight from tap JSON and is joined into the Cellar whole, so '../..' escapes. The name is less exposed because only its last slash-separated segment reaches the filesystem.
The pre-commit hook runs the test suite but NOT clippy. Run cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings yourself before committing.

All five originally-open items were closed on 2026-09-25/26. Remaining known gaps: install_from_source still delegates the actual build to brew (so clay does not build natively), and uses_from_macos is surfaced only as a source-build warning - never surfaced in `clay info`, which would be the natural follow-up.

Real index facts worth remembering (8617 formulae): all names are single-segment - no tap prefix; the core index writes itself as homebrew/core/<name> in dependency lists. uses_from_macos is non-empty on 1816 formulae and splits into ~2014 runtime strings vs ~830 object-shaped entries (bison/flex/python/zsh), which is why it is a warning and not a hard fail - a hard fail would block installs that work on Linux.

install_formula is now atomic end to end: a failure after the staging rename removes the keg (and the links, if the registry write failed), because is_installed is name-only and would otherwise report a poured-but-unusable formula as installed.

Useful test technique used here: a synthetic bottle can be built in-test with the `tar` + `flate2` deps, gzipped, placed in the download cache, and its sha256 computed - install_formula only downloads when the tarball is absent, so this drives the real install path with no network. Making prefix/bin a regular file makes link_tree fail deterministically; making registry.json.tmp a directory makes the registry write fail after the links exist.

Clay now builds formulae natively: src/build.rs fetches the source url, verifies the index checksum, unpacks, and drives autotools/cmake/meson/make. install_from_source no longer shells out to brew; --use-homebrew opts back in. The published index carries no system/install block and no patch across all 8617 formulae, so there is no Ruby DSL to interpret - that is what makes native builds tractable at all.

Out-of-tree build directory is mandatory, not stylistic: automake's configure symlinks GNUmakefile at the absolute path of the build tree, so an in-tree build creates a symlink pointing at itself and make dies with 'Too many levels of symbolic links'. This is how the first wget native build failed.

--build-from-source applies to the named root formula only; dependencies keep their bottles. Build dependencies install into a clay-owned prefix at cache_dir/build-deps, never the user's, because the default prefix is Homebrew's and linking a build dep would shadow Homebrew's own.

Fundamental remaining limit: the API's build_dependencies is incomplete (wget lists only pkgconf but really needs gnutls/nettle/p11-kit, which live in the DSL). So some formulae configure fine and then fail to compile against whatever the system include path offers - /opt/homebrew headers in the wget case. The build-failure message explains this and points at --use-homebrew.

Verified natively: portable-zlib (cmake) builds and its libz works (crc32 checked from a C program, shared and static). portable-libyaml cannot build because its own release tarball omits cmake/config.h.in.

name: brace-expansion-lockfile-fix
observations: Two live Dependabot alerts were closed BY HAND on 2026-10-01 because Dependabot refused to touch them, both reaching eslint transitively via minimatch: brace-expansion in IzonIcy/infrastructure-cost-visualizer (alert #14, 5.0.9 -> 5.0.12) and IzonIcy/UnHeard-Voices (alert #27, 1.1.18 -> 1.1.21). Commits 1cd4c38 + 27f5b68 and 0e62d65 + 42fcae3. Neither repo has a typecheck script — plain JS, lint + tests only.

CORRECTION 1 — `update-subdependencies: false` was NOT the cause. Neither repo's .github/dependabot.yml contained it; both were bare 5-key ecosystem blocks. The real reason is simply that Dependabot will not rewrite an indirect dependency's resolved version when no DIRECT parent has a newer release. It reported `conflicting-dependencies: []` — nothing was actually blocking it.

CORRECTION 2 — `pnpm update <pkg> --latest` is a SILENT NO-OP on transitive deps: it prints 'Done' and changes nothing, because --latest forces resolution outside the declared range and pnpm won't apply that to an indirect dep. What works is depth: `pnpm update brace-expansion --depth 100`. Note `--depth Infinity` is rejected by pnpm 10 — it wants an integer.

Since nothing in package.json changes (the declared ranges already permit the patched version), the real fix is a one-time lockfile re-resolve. To stop Dependabot erroring on the NEXT indirect advisory, add to the npm/pnpm ecosystem block in .github/dependabot.yml: `allow:` / `- dependency-name: brace-expansion` / `  dependency-type: indirect`. Merge it into the existing `allow:` key where one exists, matching indentation.

DIAGNOSTIC RULE: on any future `security_update_not_possible`, read the alert's latest-resolvable-version vs lowest-non-vulnerable-version. If the fixed version is newer than what npm shows as latest AND conflicting-dependencies is empty, this is the exact situation — hand-fix the lockfile with `pnpm update <pkg> --depth 100`. It looks like a hard security block but is only a resolver limitation with a two-command workaround.

name: dependabot-patched-none-lying
observations: NEVER dismiss a Dependabot alert because the API reports `security_first_patched_version: null`. That field reflects DEPENDABOT's resolver failing to find a bump, not the absence of one. Read the advisory's actual `vulnerable_version_range` and compare it against the npm registry.

Proven 2026-10-01 on IzonIcy/Portfolio: 16 open alerts, all reporting patched=NONE across two packages, and all 16 had a patched version already inside the parent's declared semver range — undici vulnerable >= 8.0.0, < 8.10.2, patched 8.10.2 against parent range ^8.0.0; fast-uri vulnerable >= 3.0.0, < 3.1.6, patched 3.1.6 against parent range ^3.0.1. One command each — `pnpm update undici`, `pnpm update fast-uri` — and all 16 closed on merge in PR #39 (squash 451c256). The lockfile was simply stale; nothing in package.json needed to change. No overrides, no dismissals, no blockers.

READ THE ADVISORY CHAIN, it tells you the answer in seconds. In Portfolio both packages sat behind deep chains — fast-uri was 5 levels down through @astrojs/check -> @astrojs/language-server -> volar-service-yaml -> yaml-language-server -> ajv. ajv@8.20.0 was already the newest release, so there was genuinely nothing to bump upstream and the only correct move was the in-range transitive.

`pnpm audit` finds what Dependabot doesn't: it surfaced SIX devalue advisories (up to high) that Dependabot never opened a single alert for, all fixed in-range the same way. Dependabot's alert set is not the whole vulnerability surface — run `pnpm audit` too.

Bare `pnpm update` with no target is a TRAP: it pulled @astrojs/react 7.x and a prettier-plugin-astro 1.0.1 -> 1.1.0 bump that would have reformatted the codebase (that repo has a commit 'fix: make prettier-plugin-astro@1.0.1 formatting idempotent' from fighting exactly that), plus TypeScript churn. Always target the package: `pnpm update <pkg>`.

WHY THIS RULE: a dismissal is a permanent security-posture record — writing state=dismissed against something actually fixable puts a lie in the audit trail, and that is far harder to detect later than a stale alert is to fix now. On any security_update_not_possible or patched=NONE: run `pnpm audit`, read security_vulnerable_version_range, check whether the fix satisfies the parent's declared range, and try that before considering pnpm.overrides and well before dismissing.

name: fork-branch-triage
observations: WHY THE OBVIOUS COMMANDS FAIL: `git branch --merged origin/main` reported almost everything as unmerged while `git log origin/main..<branch>` reported the same branches as having ZERO commits not in main. Both cannot be true. Cause: the committer-identity fix force-pushed rewritten history, so pre-rewrite branches share no merge base with main. `merge-base`, `git diff A...B` and `--merged` all report FALSE NEGATIVES on those branches.

Second trap, same day in a different form: `git diff origin/main <branch> --stat` on an old branch is NOT a measure of the branch's work. A Dependabot branch predating the npm->pnpm migration shows 'adding package-lock.json, deleting pnpm-lock.yaml' — that is the whole tree drifting since, not anything the branch did.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS — take the files the branch's OWN commits touched, then ask whether main already has them and at what version: `git diff --name-only <branch>~1 <branch>` to see what the tip commit did; `git cat-file -e origin/main:<file>` to test whether main has it; `git rev-parse <branch>:<file> origin/main:<file>` to see whether the blob matches or has evolved.

VERDICT VOCABULARY: SAFE (verified present on main, blob matches) / SUPERSEDED (main has it but since refactored — you must actually READ both versions to confirm equivalence, never assume) / HOLDS WORK (main lacks it, or has a strictly older version — keep it). Reading the surviving code matters: on athas/ai-chat-paste-images the upstream version wasn't merely equivalent, it FIXED a bug the branch had (dropped images on slash commands), invisible without reading.

COROLLARY FOR FORKS: never delete a local branch that backs an open or recently-closed PR to an upstream repo. t3code's three branches all 'held work' by this test and all back real contributions — deleting the branch doesn't close the PR, it just makes the work unpushable. Prefer `git branch -d` over `-D`; if `-d` refuses, that refusal may be the rewritten-history artifact rather than real unlanded work, so fall back to the file-level test above rather than forcing.

POSTURE: because the ancestry tools actively lie in this setup, the default has to be keep-unless-proven, and proof means reading code. A prior audit assumed ': gone upstream' meant 'already merged' and would have destroyed real work. Established 2026-10-01 across 20 branches in athas, t3code, Ai-Chef and Portfolio: 10 deleted, 4 kept, 1 real find.

name: github-display-name-squash-author
observations: Ryan's GitHub DISPLAY NAME (not the login — that is always IzonIcy) was literally `ryan` until 2026-10-01. If the author is `ryan` and the committer is `GitHub <noreply@github.com>`, that is the display name, NOT a local git config problem — so no amount of `git config user.name` fiddling fixes it.

`gh api --method PATCH user` returns `404 / needs the "user" scope`, and `gh auth refresh -h github.com -s user` is interactive. It CAN be driven from an agent session: (1) launch `gh auth refresh -h github.com -s user` as a background task so the poll survives across turns; (2) read the task output file for the one-time code (e.g. DE9E-945A); (3) drive https://github.com/login/device with a browser automation MCP — the code entry form is 8 separate one-character textboxes, so fill_form with one letter per box (the 5th box is the dash and is not fillable); (4) it advances to SUDO MODE, a genuine second factor — do NOT try to bypass it; leave the page on the user's screen and tell them to click the passkey/authenticator button, and the background poll picks up the token the moment they approve; (5) confirm with `gh api user --jq .name`.

GOTCHA: immediately after a successful `PATCH user`, a plain `gh api user` read can still return the OLD name — GitHub caches the profile briefly. Read it with a cache-buster (`gh api "user?cb=$RANDOM"`) and cross-check the public `users/<login>` endpoint before concluding the write failed. Do not re-patch on the strength of one stale read.

name: gitleaks-private-repo-pr-scope
observations: A `Secret Scan` job can fail on EVERY pull request with `403 Resource not accessible by integration` while a byte-identical workflow in a sibling repo passes. The only variable is repo visibility.

`gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v3` enumerates commits through `GET /repos/:owner/:repo/pulls/:number/commits`. With only `permissions: contents: read` declared, that call SUCCEEDS on a public repo (the PR metadata is already public, so the scope covers it) and 403s on a private repo. The fix is one line: add `pull-requests: read` to the permissions block. Read-only, and scoped to metadata the job already needed.

THE DIAGNOSTIC TRAP: the obvious move is to diff the broken workflow against a working sibling. On 2026-10-01 that diff came back EMPTY (`diff` exit 0) across Ai-Chef, Lumi-Term, LumiComp and Mist — all of which pass — which makes it look like nothing is wrong and the failure is CI flake. It is not; identical config behaves differently on public vs private repos. Check `gh api repos/:owner/:repo --jq .private` before concluding the config is fine, and read the failing run's `--log-failed` for the actual 403'd URL rather than reasoning from the workflow file alone.

WHERE IT BIT: IzonIcy/Hackathon-Ryan-June (private) had been failing this way since at least 2026-08-31, across 11 Dependabot PRs, and every one of those PRs had been merged anyway with a red X sitting there. Fixed 2026-10-01 in PR #58 (squash 941f3206); `Secret Scan` now passes on both pull_request and push. Hackathon-Ryan-June is the only private repo in the fleet with workflows, so nothing else needs the change (`machine` is private but has no workflows; `config` was private until 2026-09-30 and is now public).
WHY IT MATTERS: a permanently-red required check trains you to ignore red X, which costs you the ability to notice a real one later. A red X that has 'always' been there is the most expensive kind.

observations: OPEN, as of 2026-09-28: Ryan reports a 'file not found' dialog at macOS login. Cause still unidentified — extensive enumeration of launchd jobs, login items and shell profiles did not find it.

name: t3-statev2-db-recovery
observations: MOST USEFACT FIRST: for any "can't get in from my phone" report against T3 Code, query `auth_pairing_links` (enrollment) and `auth_sessions` (live sessions) in state.sqlite — the V1 DB, NOT the corrupt statev2 DB. This answers the question WITHOUT TOUCHING THE DEVICE. On 2026-10-03: auth_pairing_links row `<pairing-row-label>`, created 2026-10-02T23:34:07, consumed_at 23:34:12, matched the tailnet peer name <phone-node>; auth_sessions showed a LIVE phone session issued 2026-10-03T19:45Z (iOS 27.0.1, dpop-access-token) with bearer credentials expiring 2026-11-01, i.e. the phone was authenticating ~25 min before the outage and needed no re-pair.

ROOT CAUSE of the 2026-10-03 crash-loop: `~/.t3/userdata/statev2.sqlite` (543MB, the V2 orchestration projection store) was corrupt — 101 bad b-tree pages out of 132,455. The backend died with `ProviderRuntimeRecoveryError -> ProjectionStoreSetupError -> effect/sql/SqlError/UnknownError -> Error: database disk image is malformed -> ServerRuntimeStartupError: startup failed before command readiness (exit 1)`. Because it never bound, port 3773 stayed dead and `tailscale serve` proxied to a dead port — the serve config and Tailscale were innocent.

DIAGNOSTIC: `state.sqlite` (the v1 DB) passes `PRAGMA integrity_check` cleanly even while the app is crash-looping — do not stop at a clean v1 check. Enumerate ALL sqlite files: `find ~/.t3 -name "*.sqlite*" -o -name "*.db"`.

RECOVERY, verified with zero data loss beyond 3 rows: (1) `osascript -e 'quit app "T3 Code (Nightly)"'` for a clean teardown; (2) BACK UP EVERY .sqlite FIRST — non-negotiable; (3) `sqlite3 statev2.sqlite "PRAGMA integrity_check;"` to size the damage; (4) `.recover` emits SQL TEXT, not a binary DB, so you MUST pipe it into a second sqlite3 — `sqlite3 statev2.sqlite ".recover --ignore-freelist" | sqlite3 statev2-recovered.sqlite`; redirecting straight to a file yields a 469MB file failing with 'file is not a database (26)', which cost one wasted cycle; (5) set `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;` on the recovered copy, verify integrity_check = ok, then swap into place; (6) DELETE stale -wal and -shm alongside it, they are crash leftovers that poison the fresh DB; (7) relaunch, wait ~30s, confirm `lsof -nP -iTCP:3773 -sTCP:LISTEN`.

PAYOFF NUMBERS (proof it was worth salvaging): 45 tables recovered; orchestration_events 136,418 = 136,418; projection_thread_messages 9,304 = 9,304; projection_turns 1,220 = 1,220; projection_threads 176 = 176; orchestration_command_receipts 119,728 vs 119,731 (3 lost). Also secondary: the 'T3 Code (Nightly)' login item was gone so nothing relaunched at boot — re-add hidden via System Events, and check it whenever the app is mysteriously 'not running'.

PHONE-SIDE facts settled on 2026-10-03, several of which correct earlier notes: the phone is NOT too old for protocol v2 — it negotiated v2 fine, and an earlier theory that an August-era app could not speak v2 was wrong. Serve certs are hostname-bound, so `https://<mac-ip>/` fails with `tlsv1 alert internal error` and a raw tailnet IP can NEVER work — always use the FQDN. `environment-id` (<env-id>-...) unchanged since 26 May, so pairing validity survived the DB repair. Ping quality varies ~500-900ms via DERP(sfo) off-LAN and ~117ms direct over IPv6 on-LAN; both healthy. 'T3 Connect config missing' is a RED HERRING — last logged 2026-06-14, and cloudflared may run with only a loopback listener and no outbound tunnel. Also: re-pairing requires the USER to run `npx t3 pair --tailscale --label <X>` in their own terminal; it mints a 5-minute-TTL token that is a secret, so never generate or echo it into a transcript. CORRECTION — an earlier note blamed the phone failure on the Tailscale node being renamed `linux`->`<mac-host>`. That was WRONG: the node rename happened but was not the cause. The real cause was the iPhone being signed into a DIFFERENT Tailscale account, making it invisible to the Mac's tailnet; re-auth then minted a new node identity (<phone-node> -> <phone-node>) and invalidated the old pairing token, which is why the rename looked causal. A SECOND, independent failure ran concurrently: the corrupt statev2.sqlite described above. See the 'ROOT CAUSE' observation in t3-remote-access-runbook.

name: effect-cached-interrupt-replay
observations: In t3code's Effect (effect-smol, effect@4.0.0-rc.115), `Effect.cached` runs its computation INLINE IN THE FIRST CALLER'S FIBER. If that caller is cancelled, the memo records the interrupted exit and REPLAYS IT TO EVERY OTHER JOINER — peers that were never cancelled. Effect's own test suite asserts this deliberately: `.repos/effect-smol/packages/effect/test/Effect.test.ts`, case "replays the owner's interrupted exit".

Wrapping the cached effect in `Effect.uninterruptible` does NOT fix it: it stops the subprocess being torn out mid-call, but the pending interrupt is still delivered at the region boundary and lands in the memo before `cached`'s finalizer records a success. `Effect.uninterruptibleMask` plus capturing `Effect.exit` also fails — `cached`'s finalizer records the FIBER's exit, not the value you captured. The real fix is to memoize a DETACHED fiber (`Effect.forkDetach`) and have every reader `Fiber.join` it, so cancelling a reader interrupts only that reader's join.

Practical rule for this codebase: never share an `Effect.cached` read across independent request-scoped readers. If a read sits OUTSIDE a `RequestResolver` batch, a cancelled caller makes peers stop silently rather than error — a lying spinner, which this repo treats as a real defect. CAVEAT that blocked the fix on PR #14373: `forkDetach` fibers are NOT driven under `TestClock` in `it.effect`, so the fiber-memoization approach hangs the suite and cannot be verified there — the coalescing was reverted rather than shipped unverified.
